displayQuote: A man who, beyond the age of 26, finds himself on a bus can count himself as a failure

meta.title: Who really said "A man who, beyond the age of 26, finds himself on a bus can count himself as a failure"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Thatcher. The bus quip is an interwar aristocratic joke traced to the poet Brian Howard — and the original number was 30, not 26.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A man who, beyond the age of 26, finds himself on a bus can count himself as a failure'?
meta.ogDescription: There is no evidence Thatcher ever said it. The line is credited to Brian Howard and popularised by a duchess, and it said 30, not 26.

answer.label: Not Thatcher — credited to the poet Brian Howard
answer.authorDates: 1905–1958 · English poet and New Statesman writer
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Margaret Thatcher saying this. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ and states flatly that “there is no solid evidence that Margaret Thatcher ever quoted this statement with approval, or indeed shared the sentiment.” The quip belongs to interwar English society: it was popularised by Loelia, Duchess of Westminster, who — according to a letter from Hugo Vickers to the Daily Telegraph in November 2006 — admitted borrowing it from the poet Brian Howard ↗. Note the number: every documented version of the original says 30, not 26.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Two letters to the Daily Telegraph, 2 and 3 November 2006, from Alistair Cooke and Hugo Vickers
None documented; the line was attributed to her in Commons debates in 2003 and 2004

source.excerpt: Anybody seen in a bus over the age of 30 has been a failure in life.
trail: Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ records that the line was attributed to Thatcher in Commons debates on 2 July 2003 and 15 June 2004, and that a letter from Alistair Cooke to the Daily Telegraph on 2 November 2006 traced the sentiment to Loelia Ponsonby: “Anybody seen in a bus over the age of 30 has been a failure in life.” A letter from Hugo Vickers the next day added that Loelia had admitted borrowing it from Brian Howard.

Wikipedia’s article on Brian Howard ↗ independently credits Howard with coining the phrase, calls the Thatcher attribution wrong, and says it came into wider use through Loelia’s 1961 memoir Grace and Favour.
Wikipedia’s article on Loelia Lindsay ↗ agrees, describing her as having popularised the aphorism and naming Howard as the likely coiner.

We could not read the underlying evidence ourselves. The two Daily Telegraph letters and the Hansard columns Wikiquote cites are on hosts this run could not reach, so what is reported above is what Wikiquote and Wikipedia say about them, not our own reading. We have also not seen a copy of Grace and Favour, so the memoir route is Wikipedia’s claim rather than ours.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Wikiquote gives from Alistair Cooke’s 2006 letter. Wikipedia’s article on Howard prints a slightly different word order — “Anybody over the age of 30 seen in a bus has been a failure in life” — but both say 30. The popular Thatcher version lowers it to 26 and recasts it in the third person.

source.rightsNote: We cannot state a rights position honestly. The wording above is reported second-hand in a 2006 newspaper letter and in later encyclopaedia articles; we have not tied it to a specific first publication, and if the route really does run through Loelia’s 1961 memoir then that book is comfortably inside copyright. Treat the line as uncleared rather than free.

author.name: Brian Howard
author.heading: About Brian Howard
author.metaLine: 1905–1958 · English poet and New Statesman writer
author.bio: Brian Christian de Claiborne Howard (13 March 1905 – 15 January 1958) was an English poet who later wrote for the New Statesman. Educated at Eton and at Christ Church, Oxford, from 1923, he was prominent among the Oxford Wits and the Hypocrites’ Club, published verse that Edith Sitwell admired and promoted in the late 1920s, and was a key figure among London’s “Bright Young Things.” Evelyn Waugh drew on him for the aesthete who recurs in his novels.

misattribution.intro: This one is a class joke that got laundered into a Thatcher soundbite, complete with a changed number.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ states there is “no solid evidence that Margaret Thatcher ever quoted this statement with approval, or indeed shared the sentiment,” while noting that MPs attributed it to her in the Commons in 2003 and 2004.
Alistair Cooke’s 2006 letter credited her with the line, but Hugo Vickers replied the next day that she had told him she took it from Brian Howard — a chain Wikipedia repeats ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: On the best available account the words are Brian Howard’s — an Oxford aesthete’s joke about buses, as Wikipedia records ↗ — and the age in it is 30.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists this line under Misattributed for Margaret Thatcher, cites Commons debates of 2003-07-02 and 2004-06-15, reports Alistair Cooke’s 2 November 2006 Daily Telegraph letter crediting Loelia Ponsonby with "Anybody seen in a bus over the age of 30 has been a failure in life", reports Hugo Vickers’s next-day letter that she borrowed it from Brian Howard, and states there is no solid evidence Thatcher said it.

Wikipedia credits Brian Howard with coining "Anybody over the age of 30 seen in a bus has been a failure in life", says it is often wrongly attributed to Margaret Thatcher, cites Hugo Vickers writing in November 2006, and says the phrase came into wider use through Loelia’s 1961 memoir Grace and Favour. Howard lived 13 March 1905 to 15 January 1958.

Wikipedia says Loelia Lindsay (6 February 1902 – 1 November 1993) is believed to have popularised the aphorism, falsely attributed to Margaret Thatcher, which appears to have been coined by Brian Howard; her memoir Grace and Favour was published in 1961.
